newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-NZ's Peters says c/a data as expected.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-NZ's Peters says c/a data as expected.

text.p: New Zealand Deputy Prime Minister and Treasurer Winston Peters said on Friday current account deficit data released earlier had been pretty much as expected.
He told reporters in Cairns that exporters would be pleased the New Zealand dollar had come back and that New Zealand was at the bottom of a growth trough.
Earlier data showed New Zealand recorded its largest ever current account deficit of NZ$4.47 billion or 4.8 percent of GDP in the year to March 31, 1997.
The March quarter deficit was NZ$723 million, substantially above average forecasts of a NZ$212 million and the annual figure was above expectations of a NZ$4.1 billion deficit.
"The current account figures were marginally higher than predicted, but pretty much what was to be expected," he said.
Peters said the deficit reflected lower tourism earnings and smaller income for New Zealand firms operating overseas.
"It's obvious that some of our businesses abroad are not making as much as they themselves would have liked," he said.
Peters said the lower NZ dollar would help exporters.
"Exporters will be pleased that the dollar's come back," he said.
Asked about Friday's tightening of monetary conditions by Reserve Bank of New Zealand governor Don Brash who said monetary conditions were too loose, Peters would not comment.
Peters said New Zealand had improved its inflation performance after three years of struggling to stay within the target band of zero percent to two percent.
"We are comfortably within the bottom half of the expanded band of zero to three (percent)," he said.
Peters said the New Zealand economy had troughed and economic fundamentals were in place for a steady improvement.
"New Zealand's economy had traversed into a trough from late July last year, we believe we are at the bottom of that trough," he said.
"We think we'll be coming out of that, all the fundamentals are there for a very healthy growth rate."
Peters said the government would be happy with a growth rate in line with the official forecast of 4.2 percent.
Peters said a positive vote in September's savings plan referendum would be anti-inflationary and should prompt the Reserve Bank to look at monetary policy settings.
